name: Television Personalities
label: Rough Trade
lede: Dan Treacy cut a four-song EP for £22, named it after a TV host punk had embarrassed, and spent the next four decades writing songs that Alan McGee, Kurt Cobain and MGMT all fell for.

hero.by: Dan Treacy in Tokyo. Photo: Masao Nakagami

eras.title: Part-time punks on the King's Road
eras.text: Treacy was 17, living in council housing on the King's Road, with schoolfriends Ed Ball and Joe Foster for a band, when the Sex Pistols lit the fuse. His mum's money paid for the record; John Peel and Rough Trade did the rest.

years.h: Nicholas Parsons, Bruce Forsyth and Hughie Green all miss out
years.p: Treacy starts a band with Chelsea childhood friends Ed Ball and [[Joe Foster|affc8042-4575-4fc8-b59f-fb9d5d4a038a]]. The name shortlist was a run of mocked TV hosts before they settled on the generic version: Television Personalities.

years.h: '14th Floor' is the first single
years.p: The debut single gets a push from [[Joe Strummer|af4ea2a3-c54d-40b4-8120-a1f0b838ad54]].

q: My mum was hassling me to pay back the money.
years.src: Wikipedia: Television Personalities · Wikipedia: Part Time Punks
years.h: Four hours and £22 make Where's Bill Grundy Now?
years.p: Released on the band's own Kings Road label, 500 hand-pressed copies with photocopied sleeves, paid for by Treacy's mother. He mails them to labels and DJs, and [[John Peel|e4dec348-ad10-43b6-a2b1-c22aab890675]] plays 'Part Time Punks' again and again.
years.xp:
Treacy wrote 'Part Time Punks' at 17. "I couldn't believe the lyrics. Suddenly, my best friend was coming out with these amazing songs," Ball said.

Treacy had got the sums wrong on pressing costs, and the bill followed him home.

years.h: Jimmy Page hands Treacy a guitar for a jam
years.p: Page spotted Treacy reading one of his own interviews, heard he had a record out, and walked him upstairs to a wardrobe full of guitars. Five minutes later they were jamming.
years.xp: Treacy's review of the session: "He was good, but he weren't as good as me."

years.src: Wikipedia: Part Time Punks · Communication Blur
years.h: Rough Trade reissues the EP, and 'Part Time Punks' sells for years
years.p: [[Geoff Travis|70437714-3183-4916-947f-e5ba2154d16a]] takes the record to [[Rough Trade|4f4b0013-1704-4936-a769-e6e8a6e08ff8]]; the reissue sells 20,000 to 30,000, and 'Part Time Punks' as a single sells 14,000 in six months in 1980. The song even name-checks Rough Trade.
years.xp:
Treacy said the song wasn't aimed at Rough Trade or the bands it mentions, but at "the general media hype that took them into the mainstream press." Peel offered a session and was disappointed when the song wasn't in it.

Later Treacy came to see it as something of a millstone and a novelty song. Simon Reynolds called it a self-referential meta-critique of punk.

eras.title: Twiggy, Syd Barrett and Whaam!
eras.text: The first album on Rough Trade set the template: sixties pop culture, psychedelia and a voice that never pretended to be in tune. Then Treacy started his own label and made two more records in a year.

yt: 'Part-Time Punks', live at the Hammersmith Clarendon, 1980
years.h: The live debut, with Foster on bass and 'Empire' on drums
years.p: Foster and drummer Mark 'Empire' Sheppard make the band a live act, but the pair don't get on, and Foster goes. Treacy and Sheppard had helped on Foster's Missing Scientists single with Mute's Daniel Miller.

years.h: 'I Know Where Syd Barrett Lives' charts in Holland
years.p: The single sells 18,000 copies, by [[Alan McGee|ffacc13a-01e5-4b5d-a455-6a7f302ac9ce]]'s count in his 1983 fanzine.

years.src: Wikipedia: ...And Don't the Kids Just Love It
years.h: Twiggy and Patrick Macnee front ...And Don't the Kids Just Love It
years.p: Rough Trade's ROUGH 24, made by Treacy, Ball and Sheppard at Mount Pleasant in London. The cover is a 1967 photo of Twiggy and Macnee selling The Avengers fashions.
years.xp: The band produced it themselves and credited the work to "Vic Hammersmith-Broadway," a joke on the producer Vic Coppersmith-Heaven. Uncut later ranked it the 64th best album of the 1980s.
play: ...And Don't the Kids Just Love It
I Know Where Syd Barrett Lives

years.cap: Whaam! Records labels and Dan Treacy, c. 1981
years.h: Treacy starts Whaam! and signs the Pastels
years.p: Treacy's own label releases Dr & The Medics and [[The Pastels|9d6108ad-dbc2-4bf1-a746-edc1044d2749]], and the next two TVP albums.

years.h: Mummy Your Not Watching Me goes deeper into psychedelia
years.p: Treacy's Whaam! label releases the second album, with the psychedelic side pushed further forward.

years.src: Wikipedia: They Could Have Been Bigger than the Beatles
years.h: The Creation's 'Painter Man' turns up on They Could Have Been Bigger than the Beatles
years.p: Fourteen tracks on Whaam!, the 1960s cover by [[The Creation|1d5d9b06-1b0b-4c40-8481-bad62e03b4ab]] next to Treacy's 'David Hockney's Diary'. In 2011 MGMT's Andrew VanWyngarden picked it for NME's 100 Greatest Albums You've Never Heard.

years.h: Ed Ball leaves to run the Times
years.p: Ball turns his side project The Times into his main band, and in 1986 becomes an executive at Creation Records, staying until it folds in 1999.

eras.title: Barrett's address, read out loud
eras.text: Alan McGee built a club and a label partly in the TVPs' image, and the band settled into its longest line-up. David Gilmour gave them a support slot, briefly.

years.h: Jeffrey Bloom joins at a gig in Alan McGee's Living Room club
years.p: [[Jowe Head|3863fd93-5820-4574-9585-f30d71cfbaa5]], ex-[[Swell Maps|378c0556-fce5-4c1a-8360-5c48ca3e26c5]], replaces bassist Mark Flunder. After a first European tour Foster and keyboardist Dave Musker leave, and Treacy, Head and Bloom run the band as a trio for years.
years.xp: McGee's own fanzine, Communication Blur, ran a diary-style tribute to Treacy in its first issue that year, crediting Geoff Travis with seeing "the pop genius" of the band. McGee later said Treacy inspired him to start Creation Records.

years.cap: Television Personalities at the October Club, Brixton, c. 1984
yt: 'I Know Where Syd Barrett Lives', live in Germany, 1984
years.h: David Gilmour fires his support band for reading out Syd Barrett's address
years.p: Hired to open for the Pink Floyd guitarist on his About Face tour, the TVPs play 'I Know Where Syd Barrett Lives', and Treacy reads out Barrett's real address from the stage. That's the end of the tour for them.

years.h: The Painted Word slows to a drone
years.p: Released on Illuminated. Trouser Press's Ira Robbins heard spare, droning psychedelia, hauntingly beautiful like the quietest moments of the Velvet Underground.

years.h: Privilege finally reaches Fire Records
years.p: Line-up changes and circumstances held the album back for more than a year before Fire Records released it.

eras.title: Nirvana's favourite support act
eras.text: The trio recorded a whole album on four-track in a flat about to be demolished, then shelved it. Kurt Cobain asked them to open in London, and the TVPs carried on through the decade until 1998.

years.h: Fifteen songs on a four-track in Stoke Newington
years.p: Treacy and Head record over a few weeks at Head's flat in Glading Terrace, shortly before it was demolished, with a Roland drum machine and one microphone. The tapes sit for years; some songs are redone for Closer to God.

years.h: Kurt Cobain invites the TVPs to open for Nirvana
years.p: About 3,000 Nirvana fans at the London Astoria heckle the band early. The TVPs close with 'Seasons in the Sun', which turns out to be Cobain's favourite song.
years.xp:
Cobain watched from the wings. Backstage he told Treacy it was a good concert, then: "Don't let me keep you."

They met again at Wetlands in New York on July 21, 1993, where Cobain introduced Treacy to [[Courtney Love|31d2041c-985d-48f7-b6e2-2a70cdf14853]], with Debbie Harry in the room.

years.h: Closer to God mixes sixties pop with darker songs
years.p: The Fire Records album is close in tone to The Painted Word, and reworks some of the Stoke Newington four-track songs.

years.h: Don't Cry Baby, It's Only a Movie, then silence
years.p: The Damaged Goods album is the last TVPs record for eight years.

eras.title: From HMP Weare to Domino
eras.text: Treacy spent six years in and out of prison, partly on a prison ship in Dorset, then came back with Ed Ball and an album critics loved. A chaotic Brighton gig and a 2011 brain operation bracket the return.

years.h: Treacy is jailed for theft, and serves time on a prison ship
years.p: From 1998 to June 2004 Treacy is incarcerated, including on HMP Weare, a prison ship in Portland Harbour, Dorset.
years.xp: He told the New York Times in 2006: "I had a bad time. Mental illness, drug addiction, homelessness." He said he'd been in prison five times, all for shoplifting to get money for drugs.

years.src: Wikipedia: Ed Ball · Wikipedia: My Dark Places
years.h: Ed Ball comes back for the return
years.p: Ball rejoins Treacy and plays guitar on the comeback album, with Mathew Sawyer on drums and Victoria Yeulet on vocals.

years.h: The band walks off and leaves Treacy alone at the Hanbury Ballroom
years.p: Half an hour into a Brighton show, Treacy struggles with his guitars and mic stand; his bandmates leave the stage and the management stops the gig.

years.src: Wikipedia: My Dark Places · Wikipedia: Television Personalities
years.h: Domino releases My Dark Places
years.p: Recorded at Soupstudio, London, with Simon Trought. NME called it harrowing and hilarious in equal amounts; it scores 72 on Metacritic.
years.xp: Treacy admitted breaking down during the sessions: "I like to hurt when I'm working." Douglas Wolk called it the band's saddest, most chaotic album.

years.h: Treacy has surgery for a blood clot on the brain
years.p: He is seriously ill after the operation, regains consciousness in December, and stays in hospital. His most recent album had been A Memory Is Better Than Nothing (Rocket Girl, 2010).

eras.title: The lost album turns up
eras.text: Treacy was still recovering in 2016 and said he meant to make music again. His bandmates did it for him: Jowe Head's four-track tapes came out, and the old members played a benefit.

years.h: Jowe Head's 1990 tapes become Beautiful Despair
years.p: Fire Records releases the four-track album, restored from Head's original tapes, as the band's twelfth. It includes songs about [[Felt|6999f790-25f4-44a3-b745-1e3e01fde0f5]] and [[The Lemonheads|58a53082-a629-4ff1-a44d-7492d6f6e8fb]].

years.h: Former members play a benefit for Treacy at the 100 Club
years.p: Musicians from across his line-ups, with guests, play London's 100 Club to raise money for Treacy.
